title: Boots, Leather and the Road
premise: Outfit a rider for tomorrow's road: boots at Holbrook's on South Water Street, a look across the forks from Wolf Point at Miller's tannery, where the town's leather began, the saddler at Lake and Canal, and the Green Tree to lay it all out.

opening.text:
JAUNT: BOOTS, LEATHER AND THE ROAD. A spring afternoon, the mud drying at last, and you ride out tomorrow. The strangers pour through this town 'by land and by water', and most of them, like you, are 'locating farther west'. Before you join them you need an outfit, and an outfit is leather: boots for the rider and tack for the horse.

Here is the catch. In this town those are two different trades in two different shops on two sides of the river. Buy boots on South Water Street, look across the forks at the tannery where Chicago's leather began, visit the saddler at Lake and Canal, and lay it all out at the Green Tree tonight.

stops.text: Start one door east of Dearborn on South Water Street. In June 1835 John Holbrook advertised hats, clothing, boots and shoes, wholesale and retail, as agent for the manufacturers. These are made goods, shipped in from the East and sold off the shelf: in a town growing this fast, nobody has time to wait for a cobbler.
stops.narrative: Boots for the road, or a hat?

choices.label: A pair of boots off the shelf
choices.consequence: Made elsewhere and shipped in, like everything on his card. Your feet are ready for the road.

choices.label: A hat for the road
choices.consequence: The American's printing of the card puts hats first. The shoes you came in will have to do.

stops.text: Over the South Branch to Wolf Point. Across the North Branch, in 1831, John Miller built a log house on the point and used it as a tannery, Chicago's first recorded factory. Before the boats brought boots by the crate, leather here began as hides soaking in a pit. Whether hides were still worked this summer, no source says.
stops.narrative: Leather begins as hides, somewhere. Here, it began on the point.

stops.text: South down the west bank to Lake and Canal. Goss & Cobb opened here in 1833, the year Silas B. Cobb arrived, making saddles, harness, bridles, martingales and trunks to order. The partners parted in February 1835, and Cobb's June card says he will continue. Neither card names boots.
stops.narrative: Leather for the horse, or for the baggage?

choices.label: Order a new bridle
choices.consequence: Bridles are on the card. Cobb promises it by morning.

choices.label: Order a trunk
choices.consequence: Trunks are on the card too. A trunk rides in a wagon, not on a saddle.

choices.label: Ask the saddler for boots
choices.consequence: Not his trade. His card is saddles, harness, bridles, martingales and trunks; boots and shoes were Holbrook's line, back across the river.

stops.text: East along Lake to West Water and the Green Tree, which James Kinzie built in 1833 as the first house here put up for hotel purposes, 'so called from an oak tree standing close by'. Old settlers recalled Chester Ingersoll keeping it from 1834 to 1837. Lay the outfit out on the floor for the morning.
stops.narrative: Ride at first light, or wait a day?

choices.label: Ride out at first light
choices.consequence: The outfit is what it is.

choices.label: Stay a day and finish the outfit
choices.consequence: Another night at the Green Tree.

legs.note: West along South Water Street and over the South Branch to Wolf Point.
legs.story: What you bought rides in front of you.

legs.note: South down the west bank to Lake and Canal.
East along Lake Street to West Water, on the west bank of the South Branch.

endings.text: Another day in town, then. What the outfit lacks is on a card somewhere on these streets, and the road will keep. A day late is not the same as unready.

Boots from the clothier and a bridle from the saddler: leather for the rider and leather for the horse, from two trades that did not do each other's work. You ride out at first light equipped to travel.
A trunk will not ride on a saddle. The morning begins with finding a wagon going your way: the baggage is ready and the way of carrying it is not.
You ride out with what you have. Boots for the rider and a bridle for the horse were the outfit's two leathers, one from each trade; whatever is missing, the road will ask for before long.

keepsake.title: Equipped to Travel
keepsake.text: A fictional tally of one rider's outfit: what came from the clothier, what from the saddler, and what was left behind. No real sale, price or customer of either shop is written on it.

evidence.text: John Holbrook advertised clothing, boots and shoes, wholesale and retail, 'on South-Water st. one door from Dearborn street', signed himself agent for the manufacturers, and said he would be receiving additions to his assortment every fifteen or twenty days through the season; the American's printing adds hats.
evidence.locator: Chicago Democrat, 10 June 1835, p. 3, col. 2 (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c010, copy line 'Chicago, June 10, 1835'); Chicago American, 13 June 1835, p. 3, col. 6 (claim chicago_american_1835_06_13#c012). Transcription-mediated readings.

evidence.text: Holbrook's stock was made clothing sold from stock, not a tailoring service.
evidence.reasoning: An agent for the manufacturers who keeps 'a large assortment of the named articles' and restocks by shipment is selling finished goods made elsewhere. The card names no cutting, measuring, fitting or making to order, so the stop claims none; that the goods were ready-made is read from the card's words, not stated in them.

evidence.text: The store stood on the south side of South Water Street, one door east of Dearborn; the side of Dearborn is a reading and the building is reconstructed.
evidence.reasoning: Both printings give 'one door from Dearborn' on South Water Street. The structure record reads the door count as the next front east of the Chicago American's corner office under the owner's corner-ordinal ruling, because that makes three addresses printed on this face consistent; its size and form are borrowed from neighbours on the face and graded reconstructed.

evidence.text: In 1831 John Miller built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as a tannery, called Chicago's first recorded factory; Andreas has him run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern, and names Benjamin Hall, tanner, a partner of John Miller, who came in 1832.
evidence.locator: DRLOIH, 'The Beginning of Wolf Point', the 1831 sentence on John Miller's log house ('Chicago's first recorded factory'); Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), the list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, the John Miller and Benjamin Hall entries. The readings are the structure record miller_tannery's.

evidence.text: Whether the tannery was still working on 1 July 1835 is not attested; the log house is taken to stand on the scene date, and its tanyard is not modelled.
evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record miller_tannery: nothing reached follows the building past 1832, so it stands on the ordinary continuity argument and its function states what it was for, not what it was doing. The stop says so in so many words and claims no hides, pits or workers on the day.

evidence.text: The tannery stood on the north bank at the forks, on the point between the North Branch and the main stem, just north of Samuel Miller's tavern; the separation from the tavern is invented.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the direction ('just north of Miller's tavern') and DRLOIH the proximity; the structure record places the log house against this project's own miller_house record with an invented 11.5 m separation, about 40 m working uncertainty. The stop says 'at the forks' and claims no door.

evidence.text: The second stop is the scene's typed viewpoint 'The forks, from Wolf Point', on the west bank where the North and South Branches meet; the tannery as the scene places it stands about 155 m to the north-east, across the North Branch. The viewpoint is a camera position, not a claimed path or a place anyone stood.
evidence.reasoning: DRLOIH puts Wolf Point on the west bank at the forks. The anchor stands at local E -100, N -28 in data/scenes/1835.json and miller_tannery's placement at E +14, N +78, so the tannery is seen across the water rather than reached; the tannery's own place is the separate tannery-place reading.

evidence.text: Goss & Cobb advertised that they had opened a saddle and harness shop on the corner of Lake and Canal streets, making saddles, harness, bridles, martingales and trunks to order, and that repairing would be immediately attended to when brought to their shop.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), p. 3, col. 4, the advertisement headed 'Saddle & Harness Making' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c019), read from the scan; the full reading is on the structure record goss_cobb_saddlery.

evidence.text: The Goss & Cobb partnership was dissolved on 18 February 1835, and S. B. Cobb's card printed beside the notice says he will continue the business at his shop.
evidence.locator: 13 June 1835, p. 3, col. 6: dissolution notice dated 'Chicago, Feb. 18, 1835' (extracted claim chicago_american_1835_06_13#c015) and Cobb's continuation card (chicago_american_1835_06_13#c016). Transcription-mediated reading, checked against the structure record's reading of the page.

evidence.text: That Cobb's 1835 shop is the 1833 shop at Lake and Canal is reasoned, and which corner of the crossing it held is not attested.
evidence.reasoning: The American's 1835 cards keep the trade and name Lake Street but never resolve the cross street, so the structure record goss_cobb_saddlery identifies the two shops by argument and places the building on the south-east quadrant as a one-in-three choice. The stop says 'this corner' of the crossing and claims no front door.

evidence.text: Neither printing of the saddler's card names boots or shoes, and Holbrook's card names boots and shoes and no harness: on these two cards the rider's leather and the horse's leather are two trades in two shops.
evidence.reasoning: Read from the firms' own advertisements as the brief asks ('do not turn the saddler into a bootmaker'): Goss & Cobb list saddles, harness, bridles, martingales, trunks and repairing; Holbrook lists hats, clothing, boots and shoes. That the saddler would turn away a customer asking for boots is the ordinary reading of a card that does not offer them, not a recorded refusal.

evidence.text: James Kinzie built the Green Tree in 1833 as the first building in the place erected for hotel purposes; Chester Ingersoll is given as landlord 1834–1837.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 127, Green Tree Tavern: construction and landlords; DRLOIH hotel chronology, Green Tree entry.

evidence.text: The Green Tree was 'so called from an oak tree standing close by', 'one of the most noted in those early days'; it stood until 1880, when it was moved to 33-37 Milwaukee Avenue, 'where it still stands, the oldest memento of early taverns'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98792-98820 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Immigration in 1833 'assumed proportions surpassing all expectation'; the year's arrivals included John Dean Caton, Silas B. Cobb, Asahel Pierce and the Rev. Jeremiah Porter, and about 165 frame buildings went up.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12227-12245 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1834 the strangers came 'by land and by water', in prairie schooners and other wagons, 'on horseback and on foot', and 'Many immigrants passed through the town with a view to locating farther west'.
evidence.locator: p. 94, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12724-12751 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Green Tree's corner is the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, on the west bank of the South Branch, east along Lake Street from the Canal Street crossing.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record green_tree_tavern places the tavern at Lake and West Water on the owner's ruling T-0141 (position inferred); West Water is the west-bank frontage, so the leg from Lake and Canal runs east along Lake.

evidence.text: The four places are exterior stops in the 1 July 1835 scene. No interior, front door, tanner, saddler or clerk at work, keeper or customer on the day is claimed.
evidence.reasoning: Uses the structure records' own scene-date phases: Holbrook's card is dated 10 June 1835, the tannery stands on a continuity argument, Cobb's continuation card runs in June and July 1835, and Ingersoll's tenancy spans 1835. Every position is inferred. The stops speak of what each house or shop did, not of anyone met there.

evidence.text: The rider, the journey out tomorrow, the lodging at the Green Tree, the boots, hat, bridle and trunk, which was bought where, the question about boots, the decision to ride or wait, the endings, the timing inputs and the Equipped to Travel keepsake are invented connective narrative. Neither shop is claimed to have sold or made anything for this rider.
